Print the curator's message(s) at a UTC timestamp or its prefix, verbatim.

    python3 -I show.py 2026-10-12T15:53          # every message of his in that minute
    python3 -I show.py 2026-10-12T15:53:07.5     # a finer prefix
    python3 -I show.py --list 2026-10-12         # one line per message (timestamp, source, length, start)
    python3 -I show.py --count                   # how many messages the three sources give

A prefix may use a space instead of the T and may end in Z. All times are UTC.

His messages come from three places, and the header of each printed message says which:
  main  the main-session lines of the transcripts in /root/.claude/projects/-home-user-fortress/
        and /home/user/fortress-transcripts-blinded/projects/-home-user-fortress/ (the .parts
        folders included): `user` lines that are not isMeta, not sidechain, with text content
        that does not start with '<' and is not a compaction summary; deduplicated by uuid,
        because a resumed transcript replays earlier lines.
  s1    the same lines of the first coordinating session (bdff267d), read with `git show` from
        the `transcripts` branch (origin/transcripts) of this repository, 2026-08-18 to 2026-09-17.
        Skipped, with a note on stderr, if that branch is not in the clone.
  queued  a message he queued while an agent was busy that no `user` line holds as its text
        (the queue-operation `enqueue` lines and the queued_command attachments); its time is the
        time he sent it.
Nothing is filtered by author or by kind: a scheduled check-in or a pasted report that arrived as a
`user` line is printed too, so a reader decides what is his.

== later.py
later.py: his messages after an entry's creation that may bear on it, though no commit of the
entry followed them (his later word may have gone into a skill or another record instead).

    python3 -I later.py 148                   (or P-148)
    python3 -I later.py 148 --top 25          how many to print (default 15)
    python3 -I later.py 148 --at 36f7db77c --until 2026-10-21T20:54
                                              the entry's text at a commit, and no message after a time

The candidates are his messages in the coordinating sessions (tlib.COORDINATING) from the entry's
creation on (for an entry struck from POSITIONS.md, its last text is read, and the list runs on
past the removal) (the first commit of its trail that made its text), less those that leads.py already
printed near the entry's own commits. Each is scored by the entry's distinctive terms:
  - its title's words, beyond common words (a stop list, and words in more than a tenth of his
    messages), lightly stemmed (possessive and plural off, cut to 7 letters); each weighs its
    rarity in his messages, log(messages / messages holding it);
== near.py
near.py: the curator's messages in a window before a UTC time, each with the coordinating
session's message that it answered, found along the transcript's reply chain.

    python3 -I near.py 2026-09-26T10:22:23Z            window 60 minutes before the time
    python3 -I near.py 2026-09-26T10:22:23Z 15m        or 2h, 1d
    python3 -I near.py 2026-09-26T10:22:23Z 15m --cut 2000
                                                        cut each printed text at 2000 characters
                                                        (his and the coordinator's), saying so;
                                                        by default every text is printed whole

For each message of his: its time, source (main, s1, queued: see show.py), session, length and
full text. Then the message he answered: the coordinator's turn that his message follows on the
reply chain (tlib.py says how the chain is read), every text of that turn whole, each with its
time and the file and line it was read from (the first copy, when a resumed transcript replays
it). Before it, one line for each turn the chain passed over as not addressed to him (replies to
== quote.py
quote.py: does the curator's message at a UTC time hold a quote word for word?

    python3 -I quote.py "QUOTE" 2026-09-26T10:21:32Z
    python3 -I quote.py "QUOTE" 2026-09-26T10:21        a prefix: every message of his in that minute

The time is a prefix of his message's timestamp, as show.py takes it (a trailing Z is dropped).
For each message of his at that time it prints one verdict:
  EXACT        the quote is a substring of the message as stored
  NORMALISED   a substring once both have every run of whitespace made one space, ends trimmed,
               and the curly apostrophe U+2019 made a straight one (nothing else is changed)
  NO MATCH     neither; it then prints the longest run of the quote's words that the
               message holds word for word (after the same normalising), for a reader to judge
With the match it prints the message's text around it.

== trail.py
trail.py: the trail of one entry of POSITIONS.md, from the repository's history.

    python3 -I trail.py 86            (or P-86)
    python3 -I trail.py 86 --short    the commit list only, one line each
    python3 -I trail.py 86 --at REV   the record as commit REV holds it

Prints:
  1. the entry's text at HEAD (for an entry struck from POSITIONS.md: STRUCK at the top, with the
     commit that removed it and the reason its history block gives, and the text as it last stood);
  2. its blocks in POSITIONS-history.md at HEAD, each with the commit that wrote it (the oldest
     commit whose history file holds the block's provenance line). A block's own "commit X" names
     the source it cites, not its writer;
  3. every commit that made or changed the entry's text, oldest first, read from each commit's own
     tree (side branches included): hash, UTC author time, subject, what it did, how the link to
     the text before was made (number, line, title: exact; similarity: score printed), how many
== homes.py
homes.py: where a status that an entry of POSITIONS.md states may already live.

    python3 -I homes.py 151            (or P-151)
    python3 -I homes.py 151 --top 8    candidates per sentence (default 5)
    python3 -I homes.py 151 --at REV   the three files as commit REV holds them

Splits the entry (the working tree's POSITIONS.md; for an entry struck from it, its text as it
last stood, said so at the top) into sentences, and a sentence into its clauses
at the semicolons outside parentheses; a clause keeps the label that opens its sentence, as
"Built:" or "Still to build:". A clause states a status when it, its label or its sentence holds
one of the status words: built, to build, landed, pending, default, waits, standing go, listed for his
review, open, held, parked, owed, taken, stands at, returns after, not moved, and the like.

For each such clause it lists the candidates that may already hold the same point: the numbered
items of review-queue.md's lists (b) and (c), and the lines of PLAN.md (a numbered sub-line also
== pointers.py
pointers.py: every line of the record that names an entry of POSITIONS.md by its number.

    python3 -I pointers.py 86            (or P-86)
    python3 -I pointers.py 86 --at REV   the files as commit REV holds them

Searches, at the working tree: explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md, POSITIONS.md, PLAN.md,
review-queue.md, HELD.md and BOOT.md; explorations/reviews/open-asks-*.md; and every file under
.claude/skills/. The history files (POSITIONS-history.md, FACTS-history.md) are not searched:
trail.py reads the first, and both only record. A line counts when it holds the number as a word:
P-86 matches, as in "P-86's" or "(P-86)", but P-860 and P-186 do not. A line that names a range
holding the number ("P-85 to P-88") is listed too, marked as a range.
Prints path:line and the line (cut at 400 characters around the number; --whole prints it whole),
grouped by file; the entry's own line in POSITIONS.md is marked.

== comments.py
comments.py: his saved page comments that bear on an entry of POSITIONS.md.

    python3 -I comments.py 66            (or P-66)

He also comments on pages, and those comments are not in the transcripts. They are saved as
explorations/coordinator/positions-audit/evidence/curator-comments-*.md: a section per thread,
headed "## On <what it was anchored to>", with one bullet per comment, "- HH:MM: "words"".
A section counts when its heading, or a comment counts when its own words, either
  - name the entry's number, also as dictated: P-66, P66, PE66, P 66 (not P-660), or
  - quote its title: a quoted run ("..." or curly quotes) of at least three content words, at
    least 60 % of which are words of the entry's bold title (case, possessives and punctuation
    ignored).
A section that counts is printed whole, with its heading; a comment that counts in another
section is printed with that section's heading. Each with its file and line.

**The background**
- Today the interpreter decides the type of a number like `3` as soon as it reads it: a 32-bit integer (`ZZ32`).
- The compiled path doesn't. There, `3` is an `IntLiteral`: a number that hasn't picked its type yet, and becomes `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` or a float depending on where it's used.
- This morning you decided the interpreter should work the compiled path's way.

**The problem the planner found**
- When the interpreter does that, the library fails to load.
- The first break is a range like `2:46`. The library defines ranges generically: "a range over any integer type `I`".
- When `2` and `46` haven't picked a type, something has to choose `I` for them. Today neither the interpreter nor the compiler's checker can make that choice.
- Making that choice is exactly your answer 8's promotion rule: choose the narrowest type both sides convert into. That rule isn't built yet; the plan builds it in phase 3.
- So the switch can't land before the rule exists.

- Batch 6.5 goes ahead without the numeral switch. Its other four rungs (E, P, G, V) are unchanged.
- The switch moves to phase 3, into the same batch that builds the promotion rule, so each lands with what it depends on.
- What you give up: until then the interpreter keeps treating `3` as a `ZZ32`, and four ledger rows about numerals (79, 432, 437, 443) stay open. Nothing in microGPT or the tests changes because of the wait.

**Option 2** would build part of the promotion rule now, as an extra run of 6.5. It costs about 4M–5M tokens, and a worker would design part of the rule ahead of phase 3. The triage shows the rule barely moves the error count, so there's nothing to gain by rushing it.

No, I don't think you made a mistake. The two choices fit together, and here's why.

**What the JVM does:** array lengths and indices are Java `int`, a signed 32-bit number, which is `ZZ32`. Java has no unsigned integers, so there is no JVM type for a count that can't be negative. Instead, the JVM refuses a negative length or index at run time with an exception. The longest array is 2^31 − 1, about 2G elements.

**What you decided:**
- **Ranges are `ZZ32`** (27 Sept, "that's the largest array size on JVM"). This matches the JVM's `int`. Ranges must be signed anyway, because a loop like `-5:5` counts through negative numbers.
- **A size is an `NN32`** (also 27 Sept, following the specification). `NN` means natural numbers, 0 and up; `ZZ` means all integers, negative too. A size can't be negative, so `NN32` states that in the type. The same decision says the array design refuses a length over 2^31 − 1 where it makes storage, which is exactly the JVM's limit.

**So the two numbers are not supposed to be the same type.** A size says "how many", which is never negative. An index or range bound says "where", which can be negative in loops, and Fortress arrays can even start at a nonzero base index. They meet only where a size is used as a bound, as in `0#n`.

That meeting point is exactly the question on the table. Option 1 says a size converts to `ZZ32` there, the way a numeral does. It always fits, because the array design already refuses sizes over 2^31 − 1 where storage is made. If a size larger than that were ever used as a number, the conversion would refuse it, just as it refuses an oversized numeral.

**Nine steps?** I don't think this needs one. The facts are few and settled: the JVM's `int`, the specification's `NN32`, the library's own `b0#s0`, and your two decisions. They agree with option 1. **`label` is not a goto.** It's a named block that code inside it can leave early, with a value. Rust's labelled `break` with a value and Scala's `boundary`/`break` are the nearest equivalents.

```
label search
  ...
  exit search with x   (leaves the block; the block's value is x)
  ...
end search
```

`exit` can only jump to the end of a `label` that encloses it, never anywhere else. If no `exit` runs, the block's value is its last expression.

**The expected type.** Yes, Fortress works like Scala and Swift here: a block's value is its last expression, and a function's body is that expression.
- The checker carries "the type this spot needs" down into an expression. A function body gets its declared return type, and the block passes it on to its last expression.
- This matters for one kind of function. In `fail[\T\](s: String): T`, `T` appears only in the result, so the arguments can't fix it. Only the expected type can.
- Example: in `x: ZZ32 = fail("bad")`, `T` becomes `ZZ32`.
- Where nothing is expected, `T` falls back to its bound, `Any`.

**`typecase`, and what batch 11's Q2 decided.**
- `typecase v of A => e1; B => e2 end` picks a branch by `v`'s run-time type.
- Its type is the union of its branches' types, so each branch gets the type the whole `typecase` is expected to have.
- Q2 asked whether a call inside a branch gets that expected type. The batch made it so.
- You're right that we didn't go through it in detail. You accepted Q1 to Q4 at their recommendations in one answer on 10-08, around 21:40 UTC, along with the other decisions of that evening.

**`label`, Q48(a).** It's the same idea with an early exit added: the block's type is the union of its last expression and its `exit` values. The real case is `String.fss:431`:

```
verify():() = label methodVerify
    ...checks...
    typecase baseString of
        s:CatString => do ... end
        EmptyString => fail "SubString of EmptyString"
        SubString   => fail "SubString of SubString"
    end
end methodVerify
```

`verify` is declared to return `()`. The checker passes `()` into the `typecase` branches, as batch 11 made it do, but not into a `label` body. So `fail`'s `T` becomes `Any`, and the method is refused. With (a), the `label` body gets `()`, the same as any function body would.

**(b), a call that is the argument of another call.** This one isn't just unimplemented. The text doesn't describe it: the inference chapter lists "an argument of another call" under what it doesn't describe yet. The way to build it is known, though: type the argument, choose which declaration of the outer call applies, then type the argument again against that declaration's parameter. Scala does this. So I'll take your "can we measure" as the go. Once the base build is ready, an Opus worker builds it as a trial copy of the checker and measures what it clears, what it breaks, and what it costs. If the result is clean, (b) joins batch 12's checker rung before the launch at the reset.

\EXP{x \cdot 2^{k}} modulo \EXP{2^{n}}: the bits shifted out are lost, and no
\TYP{IntegerOverflow} is thrown.
So a count at or beyond the width gives \EXP{0} for a left shift, and for a right
shift \EXP{0}, or \EXP{-1} if \VAR{x} is negative.
A negative count shifts the other way: \EXP{x \OPR{LSHIFT} (-k)} is
\EXP{x \OPR{RSHIFT} k}, and \EXP{x \OPR{RSHIFT} (-k)} is \EXP{x \OPR{LSHIFT} k}.
The count is read by its value, whatever its type: an \EXP{\mathbb{N}64} count of
\EXP{2^{63}} or more is beyond the width, not negative.

\item The range \EXP{a\mathinner{\hbox{\tt\char'43}}n} is the set of
\EXP{\max(0,n)} integers $\{a, a+1, a+2, \ldots, a+n-3, a+n-2, a+n-1\}$.
This is a \emph{nonstrided} range.
If \VAR{a} and \VAR{n} are both static expressions,
then it is a \emph{static range} of type \EXP{\TYP{StaticRange}\llbracket{}a,n,1\rrbracket}
If \VAR{n} is a static expression, then it is a \emph{range of static size}
of type \EXP{\TYP{RangeOfStaticSize}\llbracket{}n\rrbracket},
even if \VAR{a} is not a static expression.
\end{itemize}

A loop whose counter must have a wider integer type runs over a range of
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} values and widens each element, as in the following
loop, where the binding converts \VAR{i} to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}
(\secref{basic-integers}):
%for i <- 0#n do
%  j: ZZ64 = i
%  ...
%end
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{for}\:i \leftarrow 0\mathinner{\hbox{\tt\char'43}}n \KWD{do}\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  j\COLON \mathbb{Z}64 = i\)\\
\(  \ldots\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)
\end{Fortress}
\revision{revival-ranges}{The Working Draft of February 2011 assumed only
that the components of an explicit range produce integer values, and named no
integer type; two of its own examples built ranges over \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64},
and a property of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} a range over \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}.
\Library\ declare the ranges over \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} alone, as the smaller
library of the compiled path already did: a range over another integer type
is a static error, and a loop that needs a wider counter widens each element
of a range of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} values.}

Non-static components of a range expression are computed in separate
implicit threads.  The range is constructed when all components have
completed normally.
